assessment.nobel_worthiness: Defect-mediated melting of two-dimensional solids via two continuous transitions with an intervening hexatic phase is exactly the kind of simple, universal mechanism that I find compelling: dislocation and disclination unbinding, controlled by renormalization-group flow, explains a messy multi-scale phenomenon with a clean model. It extends the 2016 topological-phase-transition recognition of Kosterlitz and Thouless into soft and 2D matter and has shaped colloids, liquid crystals, and film physics.
assessment.attribution: Halperin and Nelson (1978) proposed the two-step dislocation-then-disclination scenario and the hexatic phase; Young (1979) developed the independent, closely related analysis of the dislocation-mediated melting with the KTHNY name. The three-person configuration is natural and well supported by the credited names; the earlier Kosterlitz-Thouless role has already been honoured, which slightly complicates the narrative of who first identified the mechanism.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed over decades by colloidal experiments (e.g. Murray and van Winkle; Zahn, Maret and others), simulations, and liquid-crystal and film studies. Some details, especially whether melting is always two-step or can be first order depending on the system, remain debated, but the core theory is stable. Recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Simulations and experiments show system-dependent behaviour, including first-order melting in some models, so universality of the scenario is not absolute.
Overlap with the already-awarded Kosterlitz-Thouless work may lead colleagues to see this as an incremental extension.
I am relying on my own recall of the history and have not verified the details independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics give exact, general relations for the nonequilibrium work and entropy production of small systems, extending the second law to individual trajectories. This is statistical physics at its best, with simple general results valid far from equilibrium, and it is relevant to molecular machines, colloids, and nanoscale devices. The impact on theory and experiment is broad, though still concentrated in the specialist community.
assessment.attribution: Evans, Cohen and Morriss gave the first steady-state fluctuation theorem; Jarzynski (1997) the equality; Crooks (1999) the detailed fluctuation theorem; Seifert the trajectory-level framework of stochastic thermodynamics. Four credited names cover one more person than a prize allows. My selection of Evans, Jarzynski and Seifert is a judgment, and the case for Crooks is real. Credit is also shared with others (Gallavotti-Cohen, Searles, Kurchan, Lebowitz-Spohn) who are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally verified on RNA and DNA pulling, colloidal particles, and electronic systems; the theory is mathematically settled. The framework is mature, though its field-defining consequences for technology are less clear than for other candidates.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested among several overlapping contributions, and the supplied credit list cannot cover all of them.
Experimental evidence is mostly on small model systems; broad physical consequences are still emerging.
Priority questions rely on my own recollection of the literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Anyonic exchange statistics in two dimensions is a conceptually deep result: the prediction that particles can have fractional statistics overturns the boson/fermion dichotomy and underpins topological quantum matter. The theory is clean and general and has a direct route to topological quantum computation. Recent experimental braiding signatures in fractional quantum Hall interferometers and in collider geometries make it a real physical effect rather than only a mathematical possibility.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim (1977) established the idea of intermediate statistics in two dimensions; Wilczek later coined anyons, who is not among the credited names. Experimental demonstration involves Heiblum, Fève, Manfra and others, with theory by Rosenow. Six names exceed the three-laureate limit, and any three-person split must trade theory against experiment. I would pair the original theorists with one experimentalist, but that choice is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation is recent (roughly 2020 and later), with several independent platforms but ongoing discussion of interferometer artefacts and the non-Abelian case, which is not yet established. The interpretation is converging, but timing is a little early for the experimental half.
uncertainties: Non-Abelian statistics remain unconfirmed; the established evidence is for Abelian anyons only.
Interferometry results have alternative explanations that have been debated, and independent replication is limited to a few groups.
Absence of Wilczek in the credited names weakens the theory attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics established strong light-matter coupling with superconducting circuits, creating the architecture underlying superconducting quantum processors. It is a clear, general idea with rigorous theory and lasting influence. It follows closely on the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so the field was recently recognised, but cQED is a distinct and foundational step.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf (2004) proposed the architecture, and Wallraff et al. (2004) demonstrated strong coupling. Girvin is a fourth credited name; a three-person selection leaves one of Girvin or Blais out, and this allocation is unresolved. I choose Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf as the proposal-plus-experiment core, with Girvin's role as an uncertainty.
assessment.maturity: Very well confirmed by many independent groups and industrial platforms. Quantum-computing applications are still developing, but the physics is mature.
uncertainties: Allocation among Girvin, Blais, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is unresolved.
The 2025 prize on superconducting circuits may reduce appetite for another prize in the same area soon.
The practical significance depends on how quantum computing develops, which is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene created a tunable platform of flat bands with correlated insulators and superconductivity. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model is a simple, predictive theory that identified the magic angle, and the experiments confirmed it. The field of moire materials has spread broadly across condensed matter, which signals significant impact.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald (2011) predicted flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators (2018) observed correlated insulators and superconductivity. The natural pairing of theory plus experiment fits within three names, although Cory Dean's and others' contributions in related moire work, and experimental co-authors such as Yuan Cao, are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Strongly reproduced across many groups, but the nature of the superconductivity and correlated states is still debated, and the field is moving fast. Whether recognition is yet timely is uncertain; the interpretation has not stabilised.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity is unresolved.
Fast-moving field with other platforms (moire TMDs) that may reshape the credit narrative.
Possible premature recognition relative to the stability of the interpretation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gives a controlled, non-perturbative approach to strongly correlated electrons, built on the exact limit of infinite dimensions. It captures the Mott transition and is now the standard computational tool for correlated materials with DFT. It is a clean mechanism-oriented idea with decades of use.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt (1989) introduced the infinite-dimension limit; Georges and Kotliar (1992) mapped it onto the Anderson impurity model; Müller-Hartmann also contributed. The credited trio of Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt is plausible, but credit for Metzner and Müller-Hartmann is a question and neither is in the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Well established and widely validated, with cold-atom and spectroscopic comparison. It is mature, although the theory is an approximation in finite dimensions, with known limits for low-dimensional systems.
uncertainties: Missing credited names (Metzner, Müller-Hartmann) could complicate fair attribution.
Approximate nature in finite dimensions; some committee members may prefer an exact result.
Impact is mostly methodological.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Energy landscape theory with minimal frustration uses spin-glass ideas to explain how proteins fold quickly to a unique native state. It brings statistical mechanics of disordered systems to biology and fits well with a physicist's view that general mechanisms lie behind biological complexity. It is close to the interdisciplinary spirit I value, but its concrete predictive impact is less crisp than some other candidates.
assessment.attribution: Bryngelson and Wolynes (1987) introduced the spin-glass analogy; Onuchic, Wolynes and Luthey-Schulten developed the funnel picture. Parisi and others who developed spin-glass theory have already been recognised, in 2021. Credit for the protein-folding application is clear for these three, but the broader context involves others such as Dill and Go.
assessment.maturity: The funnel view is widely adopted and consistent with simulation and experiments, but is conceptual, and the 2024 chemistry prize for protein structure prediction concerned a different problem. Experimental tests of the details are indirect.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as physics rather than chemistry or biology.
Quantitative predictive power is limited relative to other candidates.
Attribution beyond the three credited names is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computation showed that quantum information can be protected in principle, a conceptual breakthrough on which all scalable quantum computing relies. Shor's code, Steane's code and Kitaev's topological codes are cleanly formulated and have wide influence. The recent experimental progress with logical qubits makes it timely, though much of the work lies in information theory.
assessment.attribution: Shor (1995) and Steane (1996) gave the first codes; Kitaev gave the toric code and topological approach. Other key contributors such as Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Preskill, Aharonov and Ben-Or are not in the credited names, which makes a three-person allocation difficult.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of below-threshold logical qubits have strengthened it, but full fault tolerance has not been demonstrated at scale. The significance for physics proper, as opposed to computer science, is a question.
uncertainties: Many essential contributors are outside the credited names.
Large-scale fault tolerance not yet shown.
Whether the committee views this as physics or computer science.
